name: Relativistic beam
description: A beam at 0.8 c. Its particles repel each other electrically, but charges moving side by side also attract magnetically: at this speed the net repulsion is only 36 % ($1/\gamma^2$) of the Coulomb force, which is why fast beams hold together. They are also harder to bend (momentum $\gamma m v$). Bring at least 90 % of the beam into the detector.

reality.represents: A relativistic beam: magnetic attraction holds it together

remarks.detail: Charges moving side by side attract magnetically, which cancels all but 1/γ² of their electric repulsion: at 0.8 c, 36 %. Fast beams hold together for this reason.
Each particle feels its own radiation's reaction (Landau–Lifshitz): with these scaled charges it radiates too much to neglect.

remarks.line: Fields from where the others are now
remarks.detail: Each feels the others' fields computed from their present motion, exact in the velocities and checked against the exact retarded fields; real fields come from where the others were a light-time earlier.

remarks.line: A beam of a few particles
remarks.detail: A dozen or so particles stand for a beam of billions: each carries the charge of many (its mass and energy scaled alike, so that its own path is unchanged), so their repulsion matches an intense beam's. The spreads are a fixed sample of the beam's distribution, the same every time.
